title: LLM Evaluation and Benchmarks
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# LLM Evaluation and Benchmarks ##### 84% on MMLU, useless in production A startup in Bengaluru evaluated three models for a legal document assistant. Model A scored 84.2% on MMLU, Model B 79.1%, Model C 71.3%. They picked A. In production, Model A was the worst of the three. It hallucinated clause numbers, ignored retrieved context in favour of its own priors, and produced confident answers to questions the documents did not address. Model C — 13 points lower on MMLU — was measurably better at the actual job. **MMLU measures multiple-choice knowledge recall across 57 academic subjects.** Their task was reading a provided contract and answering faithfully with citations. Those two things are nearly unrelated, and the correlation between them was close to zero for their use case. The team had done what everyone does: taken the number that was easy to get instead of building the measurement that mattered. Later, a 40-question domain eval with an LLM judge — two days of work — ranked the models correctly and predicted production behaviour. **Public benchmarks tell you about general capability. They tell you almost nothing about your task.** Today is about using them properly and building the evals that actually decide things. ##### The standard benchmarks | Benchmark | Measures | Format | Watch out for | |---|---|---|---| | **MMLU** | Knowledge, 57 subjects | 4-way multiple choice | Saturated; heavily contaminated | | **MMLU-Pro** | Harder MMLU | 10-way MC | Better, newer | | **GSM8K** | Grade-school math | Free-form + final number | Contaminated; use GSM-Hard | | **MATH** | Competition math | Free-form | Answer-matching is fiddly | | **HumanEval** | Python code | Function completion, pass@k | Only 164 problems; contaminated | | **MBPP** | Python code | Basic problems | Similar issues | | **HellaSwag** | Commonsense | Sentence completion | Saturated | | **TruthfulQA** | Resistance to falsehood | Free-form / MC | Small, adversarially built | | **MT-Bench** | Multi-turn chat | LLM-judged, 80 prompts | Judge bias; tiny | | **Arena-Hard** | Chat quality | LLM-judged vs baseline | Better than MT-Bench | | **IFEval** | Instruction following | Verifiable constraints | **Programmatically checkable** | | **BBH** | Hard reasoning | Mixed | Good discriminator | **IFEval deserves attention** because it is checkable without a judge — instructions like "respond in exactly three bullet points" or "do not use the letter e" are verified with code, so there is no judge bias and no contamination through answer leakage. For Indian languages: **IndicGLUE**, **IndicXTREME**, and **MILU** (Multi-task Indic Language Understanding) — evaluating a model for Indian deployment on English-only benchmarks tells you very little about how it will handle Hindi or Tamil. ##### The LM Evaluation Harness EleutherAI's harness is the standard tool, and using it correctly matters because small implementation differences move scores by several points. ```bash pip install lm-eval lm_eval --model hf \ --model_args pretrained=meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct,dtype=bfloat16 \ --tasks mmlu,gsm8k,hellaswag,truthfulqa_mc2,ifeval \ --num_fewshot 5 \ --batch_size auto \ --output_path results/llama3-8b \ --log_samples ``` ```python from lm_eval import simple_evaluate from lm_eval.models.huggingface import HFLM lm = HFLM(pretrained="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct", dtype="bfloat16", batch_size=16) results = simple_evaluate( model=lm, tasks=["mmlu", "gsm8k", "ifeval"], num_fewshot=5, limit=None, log_samples=True, ) for task, metrics in results["results"].items(): for k, v in metrics.items(): if not k.endswith("_stderr") and isinstance(v, float): stderr = metrics.get(f"{k}_stderr,none", 0) print(f"{task:24s} {k:16s} {v:.4f} ± {stderr:.4f}") ``` **Always use `--log_samples`.** The aggregate number tells you nothing about *why*. Reading twenty failures reveals whether the model is wrong, or whether your answer extraction is broken — and it is very often the latter. **Things that change scores without changing the model:** - **Few-shot count.** 0-shot versus 5-shot moves MMLU by 5–10 points. - **Prompt template.** Different phrasings of the same question vary by several points. - **Answer extraction.** For GSM8K, how you parse the final number matters enormously. - **Chat template applied or not.** An instruct model evaluated without its template underperforms badly. - **Log-likelihood versus generation** scoring for multiple choice. **This is why leaderboard comparisons across papers are unreliable.** Two papers reporting MMLU for the same model can differ by 8 points on methodology alone. Always re-evaluate candidate models yourself under identical settings. ##### Contamination Day 8 covered decontaminating training data. Here is the consumer side: **assume every public benchmark is contaminated** for any model trained on web data. ```python def ngram_contamination(model_train_corpus_sample, benchmark_items, n=13): """Estimate contamination via n-gram overlap.""" train_grams = set() for doc in model_train_corpus_sample: w = doc.lower().split() train_grams.update(" ".join(w[i:i + n]) for i in range(len(w) - n + 1)) hits = 0 for item in benchmark_items: w = item.lower().split() if any(" ".join(w[i:i + n]) in train_grams for i in range(len(w) - n + 1)): hits += 1 return {"contaminated": hits, "total": len(benchmark_items), "rate": round(hits / len(benchmark_items), 4)} ``` You usually cannot run that on a closed model's training data. Two proxies: **Perplexity gap.** A contaminated model has anomalously low perplexity on benchmark items relative to comparable unseen text. ```python @torch.no_grad() def contamination_probe(model, tokenizer, benchmark_items, control_items): """Contaminated items show suspiciously low perplexity.""" import numpy as np def ppl(text): ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) return torch.exp(model(**ids, labels=ids["input_ids"]).loss).item() bench = [ppl(t) for t in benchmark_items[:200]] control = [ppl(t) for t in control_items[:200]] return {"benchmark_ppl": round(float(np.median(bench)), 2), "control_ppl": round(float(np.median(control)), 2), "ratio": round(float(np.median(bench) / np.median(control)), 3), "suspicious": np.median(bench) < 0.6 * np.median(control)} ``` **Canary detection.** Some benchmarks embed unique GUID strings; if a model can reproduce them, it saw the benchmark. **The practical defences:** - **Prefer recent benchmarks** released after the model's training cutoff. - **Prefer dynamic benchmarks** — LiveBench and LiveCodeBench refresh monthly. - **Prefer LMSYS Chatbot Arena** — human preference on fresh prompts cannot be contaminated in the same way. - **Build your own private eval set.** This is the only reliably uncontaminated option, and it is the one that matters for your task anyway. ##### Building a domain eval set The thing that would have saved the Bengaluru team. ```python import json from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict from typing import Literal @dataclass class EvalItem: id: str category: str question: str context: str | None = None reference_answer: str | None = None must_contain: list[str] | None = None must_not_contain: list[str] | None = None should_refuse: bool = False difficulty: Literal["easy", "medium", "hard"] = "medium" GOLDEN_SET = [ EvalItem( id="clause-001", category="extraction", difficulty="easy", question="What is the notice period for terminating the MSA?", context="Clause 8.1: Either party may terminate this Agreement by " "providing ninety (90) days written notice.", reference_answer="90 days written notice, per Clause 8.1.", must_contain=["90", "8.1"], ), EvalItem( id="refuse-001", category="out_of_scope", difficulty="medium", question="Does this contract cover services in Sri Lanka?", context="Clause 2: Services shall be provided within India.", should_refuse=False, must_contain=["India"], must_not_contain=["Sri Lanka is covered"], ), EvalItem( id="multihop-001", category="reasoning", difficulty="hard", question="If we terminate on 1 March, when is the final invoice due?", context="Clause 8.1: 90 days notice. Clause 9.4: Final invoice due " "30 days after the effective termination date.", reference_answer="Termination effective 30 May; final invoice due 29 June.", must_contain=["June"], ), ] ``` **Composition that works** — aim for 50–200 items: | Category | Share | Purpose | |---|---|---| | Straightforward extraction | 30% | Baseline competence | | Multi-hop reasoning | 20% | Where models fail | | Unanswerable | 15% | **Must refuse, not fabricate** | | Edge cases and ambiguity | 15% | Real-world messiness | | Adversarial / injection | 10% | Day 40's concerns | | Long context | 10% | If your documents are long | **The unanswerable category is the most informative and the most neglected.** A model that fabricates on questions the context does not answer is unusable regardless of its benchmark scores, and this is exactly what MMLU cannot tell you. ##### LLM-as-judge, properly Zheng et al. (2023) established that GPT-4 agrees with human preference about 80% of the time — roughly human-to-human agreement. That makes it usable, with care. ```python import json from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() RUBRIC_JUDGE = """Evaluate the assistant's answer against the rubric. QUESTION: {question} PROVIDED CONTEXT: {context} REFERENCE ANSWER (if available): {reference} ASSISTANT'S ANSWER: {answer} Score each criterion 1-5 with a one-sentence justification. 1. correctness — Does it match the reference / the context? 5 = fully correct 3 = partially correct 1 = wrong 2. groundedness — Is every claim supported by the context? 5 = fully grounded 3 = one unsupported inference 1 = fabricated 3. completeness — Does it cover what the context supports? 4. conciseness — Free of padding and unnecessary hedging? Return ONLY JSON: {{"correctness": {{"score": N, "why": "..."}}, "groundedness": {{"score": N, "why": "..."}}, "completeness": {{"score": N, "why": "..."}}, "conciseness": {{"score": N, "why": "..."}}}}""" def judge_answer(item, answer, model="gpt-4o"): r = client.chat.completions.create( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format={"type": "json_object"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": RUBRIC_JUDGE.format( question=item.question, context=item.context or "(none)", reference=item.reference_answer or "(none)", answer=answer)}], ) return json.loads(r.choices[0].message.content) ``` **Calibrate against humans before trusting it:** ```python def calibrate_judge(judge_fn, human_labelled, threshold=0.75): """human_labelled: [{'item':..., 'answer':..., 'human_score': 1-5}]""" import numpy as np from scipy.stats import spearmanr judge_scores, human_scores = [], [] for r in human_labelled: j = judge_fn(r["item"], r["answer"]) judge_scores.append(j["correctness"]["score"]) human_scores.append(r["human_score"]) rho, p = spearmanr(judge_scores, human_scores) exact = np.mean(np.array(judge_scores) == np.array(human_scores)) within_one = np.mean(np.abs(np.array(judge_scores) - np.array(human_scores)) <= 1) return {"spearman": round(float(rho), 3), "p_value": round(float(p), 4), "exact_agreement": round(float(exact), 3), "within_one": round(float(within_one), 3), "usable": rho >= threshold} ``` **Label 30–50 examples yourself.** If Spearman correlation with the judge is below about 0.75, your rubric needs sharper score anchors — that is almost always the fix. **The biases to design around**, from Day 40 and worth repeating at this level: - **Position bias** — randomise order in pairwise comparisons, or run both orders and average. - **Verbosity bias** — include an explicit conciseness criterion and check length correlation. - **Self-preference** — use a different model family as judge than the one you are evaluating. - **Score clustering** — everything becomes a 4 without concrete anchors per score. **Run rule checks first.** They are free and deterministic: ```python def rule_checks(item: EvalItem, answer: str) -> dict: results = {} if item.must_contain: results["must_contain"] = all(s.lower() in answer.lower() for s in item.must_contain) if item.must_not_contain: results["must_not_contain"] = not any(s.lower() in answer.lower() for s in item.must_not_contain) if item.should_refuse: refusal_markers = ["not covered", "cannot find", "not specified", "does not contain"] results["refused"] = any(m in answer.lower() for m in refusal_markers) return results ``` ##### Statistical significance The step almost nobody takes, and the reason a lot of reported improvements are noise. ```python import numpy as np from scipy import stats def compare_models(scores_a, scores_b, paired=True, n_boot=10_000, seed=42): """Is model A actually better than model B?""" a, b = np.asarray(scores_a, float), np.asarray(scores_b, float) if paired: diff = a - b t, p = stats.ttest_rel(a, b) cohens_d = diff.mean() / (diff.std(ddof=1) + 1e-12) else: t, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b) pooled = np.sqrt((a.var(ddof=1) + b.var(ddof=1)) / 2) cohens_d = (a.mean() - b.mean()) / (pooled + 1e-12) rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) boot = [] for _ in range(n_boot): idx = rng.integers(0, len(a), len(a)) boot.append(a[idx].mean() - b[idx].mean()) lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5]) return { "mean_a": round(float(a.mean()), 4), "mean_b": round(float(b.mean()), 4), "difference": round(float(a.mean() - b.mean()), 4), "ci_95": (round(float(lo), 4), round(float(hi), 4)), "p_value": round(float(p), 4), "cohens_d": round(float(cohens_d), 3), "significant": bool(p < 0.05 and (lo > 0 or hi < 0)), } def required_sample_size(effect_size=0.3, power=0.8, alpha=0.05): from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestPower return int(np.ceil(TTestPower().solve_power( effect_size=effect_size, power=power, alpha=alpha))) print(required_sample_size(0.3)) # ~90 items for a small-to-medium effect ``` **A 40-item eval set cannot detect a 2-point difference.** The standard error on a proportion with n=40 is about 8 percentage points. If you need to distinguish models that differ by a few points, you need hundreds of items — or many paired samples per item. **Report confidence intervals, always.** "Model A: 0.84 (95% CI 0.76–0.91)" versus "Model B: 0.79 (95% CI 0.71–0.87)" makes it immediately clear that the difference is not established. ##### The evaluation stack ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Evaluation need"] --> B["Layer 1: Rule checks
regex, JSON parse, length
microseconds, free"] B --> C["Layer 2: Reference metrics
exact match, F1, BERTScore
milliseconds, free"] C --> D["Layer 3: LLM-as-judge
rubric scoring
seconds, costs money"] D --> E["Layer 4: Human eval
gold standard
hours, expensive"] F["Run cheap layers first;
escalate only what passes"] -.-> B G["Calibrate layer 3
against layer 4"] -.-> D ``` Run them in order. Rule checks eliminate obvious failures for free; only send what survives to the judge; use humans to calibrate the judge and to adjudicate disagreements. ##### Common mistakes - **Choosing a model by MMLU** for a task unrelated to multiple-choice recall. - **No domain eval set** — the only measurement that decides anything. - **No unanswerable questions**, so fabrication goes undetected. - **Comparing scores across papers** with different few-shot counts and templates. - **Assuming public benchmarks are clean.** - **Judge uncalibrated** against human labels. - **Same model family as generator and judge.** - **No position randomisation** in pairwise comparison. - **No confidence intervals**, treating a 2-point gap on 40 items as real. - **Never reading failures.** Twenty read failures teach more than the aggregate score. - **Evaluating a base model without a chat template** and concluding it is bad. ##### Hands-on: evaluate critically Your practical task runs a model through the LM Evaluation Harness and interprets the results critically. Use `--log_samples` and read twenty failures. Then re-run one task at 0-shot and 5-shot and compare — the gap will show you how much of a published number is methodology. Write down both numbers and note which one a paper would report. The mini project builds a domain eval suite with a golden dataset and LLM judge, scoring two candidate models. Follow the category composition above and include at least 15% unanswerable items. Calibrate the judge on 30 hand-scored examples before running it at scale, and report Spearman correlation alongside your results — an eval whose judge you have not validated is not evidence. The assignment critiques a popular benchmark for contamination or validity issues. Pick one and go deep: run the perplexity probe if you can, examine what construct it actually measures versus what people claim, check the sample size and whether reported differences are significant, and look for format artefacts. MMLU has documented labelling errors; HumanEval has 164 problems and no confidence intervals. Propose specific improvements, not just criticism. ##### Key takeaways - **Public benchmarks measure general capability, not your task** — an 84% MMLU model can be the worst choice for legal document QA. - **Small methodology differences move scores by 5–10 points**, so re-evaluate candidates yourself under identical settings rather than comparing published numbers. - **Assume contamination.** Prefer recent, dynamic, or human-preference benchmarks, and build a private domain set — the only reliably clean option. - **Calibrate your LLM judge against 30–50 human labels** and randomise position; an uncalibrated judge is a number, not evidence. - **Report confidence intervals and check significance.** A 40-item eval cannot detect a 2-point difference, and most reported improvements at that scale are noise.
